solution:
(i) In chlorobenzene the carbon holding the chlorine is \(\text{sp}^2\) hybridised, and an \(\text{sp}^2\) carbon is more electronegative than the \(\text{sp}^3\) carbon of cyclohexyl chloride, so it holds the shared pair more tightly. On top of that, a lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring by resonance, which gives the \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) bond partial double-bond character and shortens it. A shorter, less ionic bond means a smaller bond moment, so chlorobenzene has the lower dipole moment. Cyclohexyl chloride has neither effect available.

(ii) Alkyl halides are polar, but polarity alone does not bring about solubility — they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. To dissolve one, energy must be spent breaking the hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the van der Waals attractions between the halide molecules; the new dipole-dipole attractions set up between the halide and water release less energy than that, so the process is not favourable and the two layers stay separate.

(iii) In a Grignard reagent the \(\text{C}-\text{Mg}\) bond is highly polar with the carbon carrying a large partial negative charge, so the reagent behaves as a carbanion and is a very strong base. It therefore reacts with even traces of moisture, being protonated to the alkane:
\(\text{RMgX} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RH} + \text{Mg}(\text{OH})\text{X}\)
The reagent is destroyed before it can be used, so it must be made and kept under anhydrous conditions. For the same reason it reacts with any compound carrying an acidic hydrogen.

Freon 12 (dichlorodifluoromethane, \(\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2\)) — the commonest refrigerant in refrigerators and air conditioners, and formerly a propellant in aerosol sprays. Its use is being phased out because chlorofluorocarbons deplete the ozone layer.

DDT (\(p,p'\)-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) — an insecticide, used chiefly against the mosquitoes and lice that carry malaria and typhus. It is not readily biodegradable and accumulates in fatty tissue, so its use is now restricted.

Carbon tetrachloride (\(\text{CCl}_4\)) — a solvent for oils, fats and waxes, used in dry cleaning and as a starting material for refrigerants and propellants; it was once used in fire extinguishers under the name pyrene.

Iodoform (\(\text{CHI}_3\)) — formerly used as an antiseptic for dressing wounds. Its antiseptic action is due to the free iodine it liberates, not to the compound itself, and its objectionable smell has led to its replacement by other antiseptics.

(i) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I}\) (1-iodopropane) — the Finkelstein exchange; \(\text{NaCl}\) is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, driving the equilibrium forward.

(ii) \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2\) (2-methylprop-1-ene) — with ALCOHOLIC \(\text{KOH}\) the ethoxide ion acts as a base and removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen, so a tertiary halide gives elimination rather than substitution.

(iii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) (butan-2-ol) — in AQUEOUS \(\text{NaOH}\) the hydroxide ion behaves as a nucleophile and substitution wins.

(iv) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}\) (propanenitrile) — the ionic cyanide attacks through carbon, so the nitrile is the main product.

(v) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5\) (ethoxybenzene, ethyl phenyl ether) — a Williamson synthesis: the phenoxide oxygen attacks the primary halide.

(vi) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\) (1-chloropropane), together with \(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{HCl}\), both of which escape as gases and leave a pure product.

(vii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) (1-bromobutane) — in the presence of peroxide the addition is anti-Markovnikov, so the bromine goes to the terminal carbon.

(viii) \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) (2-bromo-2-methylbutane) — ordinary Markovnikov addition: the hydrogen adds to the double-bond carbon already carrying more hydrogen, and the bromine to the other, which also gives the more stable tertiary carbocation.

n-Butyl bromide is a PRIMARY halide, so the reaction goes by the bimolecular \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) route in a single step with no intermediate.

The cyanide ion attacks the carbon carrying the bromine from the side directly opposite the \(\text{C}-\text{Br}\) bond. As it approaches, the \(\text{C}-\text{CN}\) bond begins to form while the \(\text{C}-\text{Br}\) bond begins to break, and the molecule passes through a transition state in which the carbon is bonded partially to both groups and the three hydrogens (and alkyl group) lie in a plane:

\(\text{NC}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{Br} \rightarrow [\text{NC}\cdots\text{CH}_2(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7)\cdots\text{Br}]^{\ddagger} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-\)

Because the making and breaking of bonds happen together, both species appear in the rate-determining step and the reaction follows second-order kinetics:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}][\text{CN}^-]\)

The backside attack also means the configuration at that carbon is inverted, which would be observable if the carbon were a stereocentre. Since \(\text{KCN}\) is ionic and provides free cyanide ions, attack occurs through carbon and the product is the nitrile, n-butyl cyanide.

\(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) reactivity is governed by how crowded the carbon under attack is, so it falls as substitution at that carbon and at the carbon next to it increases.

(i) 1-Bromopentane (1\(^\circ\)) \(>\) 2-Bromopentane (2\(^\circ\)) \(>\) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (3\(^\circ\)).

(ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane (1\(^\circ\)) \(>\) 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane (2\(^\circ\)) \(>\) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (3\(^\circ\)).

(iii) All four are primary, so the order is decided by branching at the \(\beta\)-carbon — the nearer and the more numerous the branches, the greater the hindrance to backside attack:
1-Bromobutane (unbranched) \(>\) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane (branch two carbons away) \(>\) 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane (branch on the \(\beta\)-carbon) \(>\) 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (two branches on the \(\beta\)-carbon; this neopentyl halide is almost inert to \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\)).

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHClC}_6\text{H}_5\) is hydrolysed more easily.

Both compounds are benzylic halides, and with aqueous alkali they react through the \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) route, whose slow step is the loss of chloride to give a carbocation. The rate therefore follows the stability of that carbocation.

The ion from \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHClC}_6\text{H}_5\) is the diphenylmethyl cation, in which the positive charge is delocalised over TWO benzene rings, whereas the ion from \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\) is the benzyl cation, delocalised over only one. The extra ring gives a much larger number of resonance structures and a correspondingly more stable cation, which is formed faster.

Hence \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHClC}_6\text{H}_5\) is hydrolysed more readily by aqueous \(\text{KOH}\).

Melting a solid means breaking up its crystal lattice, so the melting point depends on how well the molecules pack together, not simply on their polarity or molecular mass — and all three dichlorobenzenes have the same mass.

The para isomer is the most symmetrical of the three: its two chlorine atoms lie on opposite corners of the ring, giving a molecule that fits neatly and closely into the crystal lattice. The ortho and meta isomers are less symmetrical, pack less efficiently and leave more space between molecules, so their lattices are held together less strongly.

A more closely packed lattice needs more energy to break, and therefore \(p\)-dichlorobenzene melts at a higher temperature than the \(o\)- and \(m\)-isomers.

Note that the same argument does NOT apply to boiling points, which depend on the attractions between molecules in the liquid rather than on lattice packing — the three isomers boil at very similar temperatures. The greater symmetry of the para isomer also makes it the least soluble of the three.

(i) Propene to propan-1-ol — the peroxide effect puts the halogen on the terminal carbon:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(ii) Ethanol to but-1-yne:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 443\,\text{K}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2} \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH, then NaNH}_2} \text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}\), then \(\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} \xrightarrow{\text{NaNH}_2} \text{HC}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+ \xrightarrow{\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}\)

(iii) 1-Bromopropane to 2-bromopropane — eliminate, then add back the other way round:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr (no peroxide)}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3\)

(iv) Toluene to benzyl alcohol:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Cl}_2,\ \text{UV light}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(v) Benzene to 4-bromonitrobenzene — the ORDER matters: brominate first, because bromine is \(o,p\)-directing, whereas a nitro group introduced first would be meta-directing and give the wrong isomer:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2,\ \text{anhyd. FeBr}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. HNO}_3 + \text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2\)

(vi) Benzyl alcohol to 2-phenylethanoic acid — the nitrile adds the extra carbon:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_2} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\)

(vii) Ethanol to propanenitrile:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{PBr}_3} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KCN}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN}\)

(viii) Aniline to chlorobenzene — the Sandmeyer reaction:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl},\ 273-278\,\text{K}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{N}_2\)

(ix) 2-Chlorobutane to 3,4-dimethylhexane — Wurtz coupling of two sec-butyl groups:
\(2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaCl}\)

(x) 2-Methyl-1-propene to 2-chloro-2-methylpropane — straightforward Markovnikov addition:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}\)

(xi) Ethyl chloride to propanoic acid:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KCN}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\)

(xii) But-1-ene to n-butyl iodide — two steps, because \(\text{HI}\) shows no peroxide effect and would add by Markovnikov's rule:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{NaI, dry acetone}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I}\)

(xiii) 2-Chloropropane to 1-propanol:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(xiv) Isopropyl alcohol to iodoform — the haloform reaction, which works because the alcohol carries a \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\) group:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHOH} \xrightarrow{\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{CHI}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\)

(xv) Chlorobenzene to \(p\)-nitrophenol — nitrating first is essential, since the nitro group is what activates the ring towards nucleophilic displacement of the chlorine:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 373\,\text{K}} p\text{-ClC}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH},\ 443\,\text{K}} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} p\text{-HOC}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2\)

(xvi) 2-Bromopropane to 1-bromopropane:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\)

(xvii) Chloroethane to butane — Wurtz:
\(2\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaCl}\)

(xviii) Benzene to diphenyl — Fittig:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Cl}_2,\ \text{anhyd. AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}\), then \(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + 2\text{NaCl}\)

(xix) tert-Butyl bromide to isobutyl bromide — eliminate to the alkene, then re-add the halogen the other way round using the peroxide effect:
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\)

(xx) Aniline to phenyl isocyanide — the carbylamine reaction:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NC} + 3\text{KCl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
_note: Several of these conversions turn on the SAME point and are worth reading together: HBr is the only hydrogen halide that shows the peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect, which is why (i), (xii), (xiii), (xvi) and (xix) all route through HBr/peroxide rather than adding HI or HCl directly. Items (v) and (xv) turn instead on the ORDER of two aromatic substitutions.

solution:
The difference is not in the potassium hydroxide but in what the solvent leaves available to react.

In AQUEOUS solution \(\text{KOH}\) is almost completely ionised and supplies hydroxide ions. The hydroxide ion is a good nucleophile, so it attacks the carbon carrying the halogen and displaces it, giving the alcohol by nucleophilic substitution:
\(\text{R}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} + \text{aq. KOH} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} + \text{KCl}\)

In ALCOHOLIC solution the \(\text{KOH}\) reacts with the alcohol to give alkoxide ions, \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\). The alkoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide but a poorer nucleophile towards carbon, and being bulkier it reaches a \(\beta\)-hydrogen more easily than the crowded carbon atom. It therefore abstracts a \(\beta\)-hydrogen while the halide ion leaves, giving the alkene by elimination:
\(\text{R}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} + \text{alc. KOH} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{KCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Water also solvates the hydroxide ion strongly through hydrogen bonding, which lowers its basicity and further favours substitution in the aqueous medium.

The decisive clue is the last one. \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}\) has two primary isomers, n-butyl bromide and isobutyl bromide; since the Wurtz product (d) is stated to DIFFER from the one n-butyl bromide gives, (a) must be the other primary isomer.

(a) is isobutyl bromide, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\).

Checking this against the other two clues:

With alcoholic \(\text{KOH}\) it loses \(\text{HBr}\) to give the alkene (b):
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{KBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
(b) is 2-methylprop-1-ene.

Adding \(\text{HBr}\) back to (b) follows Markovnikov's rule, so the bromine now goes to the more substituted carbon:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}\)
(c) is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, tert-butyl bromide — which is indeed an isomer of (a), as required.

With sodium it undergoes Wurtz coupling:
\(2(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + 2\text{NaBr}\)
(d) is 2,5-dimethylhexane, \(\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}\) — different from the n-octane that n-butyl bromide would have given, exactly as the question states.

(a) = \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\); (b) = \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2\); (c) = \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}\); (d) = 2,5-dimethylhexane.

(i) n-Butyl chloride with alcoholic \(\text{KOH}\) — the alkoxide removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen, so dehydrohalogenation gives an alkene:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{KCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(ii) Bromobenzene with magnesium in dry ether — a Grignard reagent is formed:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}\) (phenylmagnesium bromide)

(iii) Chlorobenzene on hydrolysis — aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution because the \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) bond has partial double-bond character, so very drastic conditions are needed. Heating with aqueous \(\text{NaOH}\) at about \(623\,\text{K}\) and \(300\) atmospheres gives sodium phenoxide, and acidification then gives phenol:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH},\ 623\,\text{K},\ 300\,\text{atm}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)

(iv) Ethyl chloride with aqueous \(\text{KOH}\) — the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile and substitution gives the alcohol:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{aq. KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{KCl}\)

(v) Methyl bromide with sodium in dry ether — the Wurtz reaction joins the two methyl groups:
\(2\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaBr}\) (ethane)

(vi) Methyl chloride with \(\text{KCN}\) — the ionic cyanide attacks through carbon, giving the nitrile:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{KCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CN} + \text{KCl}\) (methyl cyanide, ethanenitrile)
